course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Properties of Materials
unit.blurb: Physical and chemical properties of materials, how metals and non-metals differ, and why alloys are harder than pure metals.

O1.t: Describe physical properties: strength, hardness, ductility, malleability, melting point, conductivity and density.

O2.t: Describe chemical properties: reactivity, flammability, acidity, corrosiveness and toxicity.

O3.t: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals, including exceptions such as carbon.

O4.t: Explain why alloys have different properties from pure metals and give uses of alloys.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 7: Properties of Materials.

The first aeroplane, built in 1903, was made of wood and fabric. Today's jets use aluminium and titanium alloys, carbon fibre and plastics: light, strong and long-lasting. What properties make these materials so useful? Let's find out!
Look at a diamond. Is it shiny or dull? Hard or soft? Warm or cold to the touch? When you answer, you are describing its properties: the way a material behaves.
Physical properties can be measured or observed without changing the substance, often using our senses. They include strength, hardness, melting point, conductivity and density.
Chemical properties can only be observed when the material reacts with another substance, and it may become something new. They include reactivity, flammability, acidity and toxicity.

Strength is how well a material withstands forces or supports weight without breaking. If we knock a glass jug and a metal jug against a hard surface, the glass cracks, but the metal jug survives. The metal is stronger.
Hardness means not being easily scratched. A nail scratches a plastic bowl, but not a metal bowl, so the metal is harder than the plastic.
The Mohs scale rates hardness from 1, the softest, talc, to 10, the hardest, diamond. A mineral can scratch anything with a lower number.
Everyday objects fit on the scale too: a fingernail is about 2.5, glass about 5.5, a steel nail 6.5, and a drill bit 8.5.
A material is ductile if it can be stretched into wires without breaking. Gold and copper are very ductile.
A material is malleable if it can be hammered or rolled into a new shape. Aluminium is rolled into foil, and metals are hammered into tools, horseshoes and jewellery.
A material is flexible if it bends without breaking. Metal wire is flexible, but a pencil snaps, so it is not.
The melting point is the temperature at which a substance melts, and the boiling point is the temperature at which it boils. Different substances have very different values.
Nitrogen boils at minus 196 degrees Celsius, so at room temperature it is a gas. Water melts at 0 and boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
Gold melts at 1064 degrees, and aluminium boils at a scorching 2480 degrees Celsius!
Most metals have high melting points, which is why they are solid at room temperature. Liquid nitrogen is so cold that it boils as soon as it is poured, freezing whatever it touches.
We use many electrical devices every day, so they must contain materials that conduct electricity. Copper is used in wires because it is a good conductor, and it's ductile too.
Electricity can be dangerous, so wires are covered with plastic, an electrical insulator, which stops electricity passing through and protects us from shocks.
Imagine leaving a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in a pot of boiling pasta. Which gets hot first?
The metal spoon! Most metals are good thermal conductors. Wood, plastic and silicone are thermal insulators, which is why cooking utensils are made from them.
Two blocks, each one cubic centimetre: one silver and one wood. Which is heavier? The silver block has a mass of 10.5 grams, but the wood only 0.9 grams.
Density measures how much matter is packed into a space. Silver has more atoms in each cubic centimetre, so it is denser than wood.
Very dense materials, like most metals, sink in water, while less dense materials, like wood, float.
So why don't steel ships sink? Think about all the air inside the hull, which makes the ship as a whole less dense than water.

captions: Iron is hard and strong. But in wet conditions it combines with oxygen to form a flaky, red-brown substance: iron oxide, or rust. Rusting is a chemical property of iron, so pure iron is a poor choice outdoors.
Reactivity describes how easily a material reacts. Sodium, a soft shiny metal, is so reactive that it reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen gas.
The opposite of reactive is inert. Gold is very unreactive: it doesn't react with air, so it stays shiny, which makes it perfect for jewellery. Inert gases are also used inside some lamps.
Flammability is the ability to burn. When wood burns, it combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. Fuels like petrol are flammable too.
Many substances are acidic or alkaline. The pH scale runs from 0, very acidic, through 7, neutral, to 14, very alkaline. Lemon juice is acidic, while many household cleaners are alkaline.
Corrosive substances destroy materials, including living tissue, on contact. Batteries left too long in a device can leak corrosive substances.
Toxicity is how poisonous a substance is. Pesticides kill insects but can harm people and the environment. Lead, arsenic and mercury are toxic elements that harmed people in the past.

captions: Elements are classified as metals or non-metals. Most elements are metals, like iron, silver and copper. There are fewer non-metals, but they combine to form plastics, sugar, water and petrol.

Metals are usually solid at room temperature with high melting points, they conduct electricity and heat, and they are shiny. Non-metals are often gases with low melting points, they are insulators, and they are dull.
Metals are malleable, ductile, strong and dense. Non-metals are usually brittle, weak and less dense.
There are exceptions! Diamond is a form of carbon, a non-metal. But unlike most non-metals, it is shiny, extremely hard and has a very high melting point.
Graphite, used in pencils, is also carbon. It has a high melting point and, unusually for a non-metal, it conducts electricity. But it is soft and brittle.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Their atoms are joined in different ways, so their properties are very different.

sections.title: Alloys

stops.note: Paused after: “That makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals, and cracks don't spread through th”
Paused after: “Titanium alloy is strong, light, resists corrosion and is not toxic, so it's used in aircr”

captions: In a pure metal, all the atoms are the same size and are arranged in neat layers. Push hard enough, and the layers slide over each other. That's why pure metals are malleable and ductile, but also quite soft.
An alloy is a mixture, so it has atoms of different sizes. The layers are no longer regular, so they can't slide easily.
That makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals, and cracks don't spread through them so easily. You can model this with towers of same-sized bricks and mixed-sized bricks!

Alloys can be designed with exactly the properties we need. Bronze, copper mixed with tin, is much stronger than either metal alone. It was first used about 5300 years ago, giving its name to the Bronze Age.

Stainless steel contains iron, chromium, nickel and carbon; it is shiny, strong and doesn't rust, so it's used for sinks and cutlery. Sterling silver, silver mixed with copper, is harder than soft pure silver.

Titanium alloy is strong, light, resists corrosion and is not toxic, so it's used in aircraft, racing bikes and hip implants. In 2023, Australian scientists developed a cheaper titanium alloy using oxygen and iron.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: A drill bit can scratch a mirror. Which property is being tested? Pause the video now.
Answer: Hardness.
Question 2: Which two properties make copper good for electrical wires? Pause the video now.
Answer: It is a good electrical conductor and it is ductile.
Question 3: Is flammability a physical or a chemical property? Pause the video now.
Answer: Chemical – burning makes new substances.
Question 4: Use the particle model: why is an alloy harder than a pure metal? Pause the video now.
Answer: Different-sized atoms stop the layers from sliding over each other.
